subject: chemistry_2
question_text: What are interhalogen compounds? Give some examples to illustrate the definition. How are they classified?

verification.note: Unit 9 (VIIA Group Elements) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.87-88, the sub-box "VIIA GROUP ELEMENTS" of printed chapter 7, which prints the question and a model answer including the AX/AX3/AX5/AX7 table on book p.88. The 1+1+2 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. The printed table was checked in full and its chemistry is correct: sp3 linear, sp3d T-shaped, sp3d2 square pyramidal, sp3d3 pentagonal bipyramidal. Both printed equations were atom-counted and balance as printed. BOOK GAPS: the printed answer never says which halogen takes the central place, never says why n is always odd, and never states that interhalogens are more reactive than the halogens except fluorine; all three are written here. BOOK NOTATION: hybridisation is printed "SP3"; it is written sp3 here. NOTE ON ICl3: the book lists it as an AX3 example, which is how the formula is taught, but it exists as the dimer I2Cl6 in the solid; that is recorded in the classification step's why and kept off the answer lines. FIGURE SCOPE: the question asks how they are classified, not for a drawing, and each type is fully named by its shape word, so no figure is authored on this card.

steps.label: What they are
lines: A is the larger, less electronegative halogen
and X is the smaller, more electronegative
one. The number n is always odd.
steps.why: Only two elements are present, so the compound is binary. The larger halogen takes the central place because it has empty d orbitals it can use and room for more atoms around it. The number of X atoms it can hold grows as the size difference grows, which is why IF₇ exists but ClF₇ does not.
common_mistakes: Giving Cl₂ or F₂ as an example. An interhalogen must contain two different halogens.
Writing that the smaller halogen is central. The larger, less electronegative one is central.
steps.memory_tip: Bigger halogen in the middle, smaller ones around it, and always an odd number of them.
steps.margin_note: The words binary, two different halogens and the formula AXn are what carry this mark.

steps.label: Examples and equations
lines: Examples: ClF, BrF, ICl, ClF₃, BrF₃, ClF₅,
Interhalogens are more reactive than the
halogens, because the A–X bond is weaker
Fluorine is the exception: F₂ is more
steps.why: The two equations show that the type depends on how much fluorine is supplied: equal volumes give ClF, an excess of fluorine gives ClF₃. Both balance, with 2 Cl and 2 F in the first and 2 Cl and 6 F in the second. The A–X bond is between two different atoms and is weaker than the bond in either halogen, which is why these compounds react readily.
common_mistakes: Writing ClF₂ or IF₆. Only odd numbers of X atoms occur, so the formulae are ClF, ClF₃, ClF₅ and IF₇.
Writing that interhalogens are more reactive than every halogen. F₂ is more reactive than any of them.
steps.memory_tip: Equal volumes give ClF, excess fluorine gives ClF₃. More fluorine, more fluorine atoms in the product.
steps.margin_note: Two or three named examples plus one equation earn this mark. Choose examples from different types.

steps.label: The four types with shapes
lines: They are classified by the number of X
atoms around the central atom A.

lines.text: AX : sp³, linear — ClF, BrF, ICl

lines: AX₃ is trigonal bipyramidal with two lone
pairs, and AX₅ is octahedral with one lone
pair, which is why their shapes are T and
steps.why: The central atom unpairs one, two or three of its electron pairs into empty d orbitals, so the hybridisation runs sp³, sp³d, sp³d², sp³d³ and the number of X atoms runs 1, 3, 5, 7. Two of the shapes are not the parent shape: AX₃ starts from a trigonal bipyramid and loses two positions to lone pairs, and AX₅ starts from an octahedron and loses one. ICl₃ is listed as an AX₃ formula in the book, and it is worth knowing that it exists as the dimer I₂Cl₆ in the solid.
common_mistakes: Writing the AX₃ shape as trigonal planar or trigonal pyramidal. It is T-shaped, because two of the five positions hold lone pairs.
Writing AX₅ as trigonal bipyramidal. Five bonds and one lone pair give a square pyramid.
Giving the hybridisation without the shape, or the shape without the hybridisation. Both halves are marked.
steps.memory_tip: One, three, five, seven X atoms, and sp³, sp³d, sp³d², sp³d³ in the same order.
steps.margin_note: Two marks sit here, so set the four types out as four separate lines with type, hybridisation, shape and one example on each.

insider_note: Half the marks on this question are in the four-line classification, so write it as four lines and put type, hybridisation, shape and example on each one.
